title: Data Lab SQL read-only enforcement bypassed via MySQL executable comments and comment-stripping empty-statement trick → arbitrary DDL/DML
failure_scenario: The validator strips /* ... */ comments to build `cleanQuery`, but the ORIGINAL `query` is what is sent to MySQL (connection.query(query), multipleStatements:true at line 650). MySQL executes the contents of `/*! ... */` version-comments. Payload: `/*!40000 DROP TABLE users */` — the comment strip makes cleanQuery empty, so `statements` is [] and the for-loop performs ZERO checks (no forbidden-keyword test, no allowed-prefix test), the request passes, and MySQL executes `DROP TABLE users`. Variant with a leading benign statement: `SELECT 1;/*!40000 DELETE FROM accounts */` → validator sees only `SELECT 1`, MySQL runs the DELETE. This defeats the 'Only read-only queries are allowed' guarantee
impact: Complete bypass of the advertised read-only guard on the customer's MySQL/PlanetScale connector: arbitrary DROP/DELETE/UPDATE/INSERT, including by users holding the 'viewer' role who are denied write access on every other storage endpoint.
checked_mitigations: Confirmed the read-only block (lines 135-173) is the only gate and operates on the comment-stripped `cleanQuery` while execution uses the untouched `query`; confirmed multipleStatements:true is unconditionally set for the MySQL path (line 650) and IAM path (line 365); confirmed no `access.role === 'viewer'` rejection exists in this route (grep shows role only used for masking at line 943).

title: Data Lab read-only guard misses Postgres 'SELECT ... INTO' — allows table creation / writes through a SELECT-prefixed query
evidence:
const forbiddenKeywords = ['INSERT','UPDATE','DELETE','DROP','ALTER','CREATE','REPLACE','TRUNCATE', ... 'INTO OUTFILE','INTO DUMPFILE','LOCK','UNLOCK'];
const allowedPrefixes = ['SELECT','SHOW','DESCRIBE','EXPLAIN','DISCOVER_SCHEMA','WITH'];
failure_scenario: The forbidden list only blocks the literal phrases 'INTO OUTFILE' and 'INTO DUMPFILE', not a bare INTO, and does not treat `SELECT ... INTO` as a write. Payload: `SELECT * INTO exfil_copy FROM users` — statement starts with the allowed prefix SELECT, contains no forbidden keyword (the token is INTO, not CREATE), passes the guard, and Postgres executes it as a CREATE-TABLE-AS, writing a new table. Similarly `SELECT pg_read_file('/etc/passwd')` / `SELECT lo_export(...)` pass as they are function calls behind a SELECT prefix. This defeats the read-only guarantee for the Postgres/Supabase connector, again exploitable by a 'viewer'.
impact: Read-only enforcement bypass on customer Postgres: attacker can materialize tables (data duplication/exfiltration staging) and invoke write/file/large-object functions, all through a query the guard classifies as read-only.
checked_mitigations: Read forbiddenKeywords (lines 140-144) and confirmed no bare 'INTO' and no handling of SELECT...INTO; confirmed allowedPrefixes accepts 'SELECT' (line 145) so the statement is admitted; confirmed the admitted query is passed unchanged to client.query at line 563.

title: All response headers from the tenant app, including Set-Cookie, are copied back to the browser on the Deployify origin
failure_scenario: 'set-cookie' is not in skipHeaders. Attacker deploys an app that answers with `Set-Cookie: deployify_session=<JWT the attacker minted for their own account>; Path=/`. A victim who loads https://deployify.io/api/v1/proxy/evil/anything (a plain image/link works, the header is applied on any response) gets that cookie written for the apex host, overwriting their own session. When the victim then goes to the dashboard they are silently operating inside the attacker's account and will connect repositories, paste env secrets and add payment methods there. The same primitive works from a project subdomain with `Domain=.deployify.io`, since a cookie scoped to the parent domain is accepted from slug.
impact: Session fixation / cookie tossing on the primary application domain: victims are forced into an attacker-controlled session (credential and source-code theft), or arbitrary apex cookies are overwritten to break CSRF/state handling. Any tenant can do this to any Deployify user.
checked_mitigations: Read the whole handler: no filtering of set-cookie, no cookie rewriting, no domain scoping. src/lib/auth.ts sets the session cookie with path '/' and no Domain, so a same-name host-only cookie written by this path collides with and can shadow the real one. Nothing in src/proxy.ts strips Set-Cookie from downstream responses.
